# Tracking and ranging from a drone camera, with honest uncertainty, on a laptop CPU

*Computer vision and robotics perception.*

## Abstract

I built a pipeline that takes drone-camera video, detects and tracks people and vehicles, estimates how far away each one is with an error bar, and runs on a laptop CPU. On synthetic flights with exact truth and poses, estimating the ground from the drone's motion gave a median distance error of 2.4%, against 14.7% for flat ground given the true height; one estimate in ten was more than 35% off. With assumed typical navigation errors the median rose to 12% (flat ground: 40%). After calibration, 90 % error bars held only 84% of the time. On real footage, parked vehicles' positions repeated within 7.6% of range. It runs at 9.6 frames per second, or 33 at lower accuracy.

## Problem

A camera gives direction, not distance. To turn a pixel into a range, I need to know where the ground is relative to the camera, and every error in height, attitude or ground shape becomes a range error that grows towards the horizon. So I wanted the system to report not only a range but how far to trust it, and to say when not to trust it at all.

## Method

1. **Detect and track.** I fine-tuned a YOLO26n detector on VisDrone2019 and used the BoT-SORT tracker with camera-motion compensation. I left out appearance re-identification on purpose: the tracker uses motion and overlap only.
2. **Range.** I cast a ray from the camera through each box's ground-contact point and intersect it with the ground. The ground is either a flat plane or a local surface I triangulate from image features tracked across frames, using the drone's known poses (terrain from motion). I chose the second because the first needs the height above the ground, which a real drone does not know.
3. **Uncertainty.** I propagate sensor noise to first order and by Monte Carlo, calibrate the intervals on separate flights (split conformal prediction), and train a small reliability flag on features I can explain.
4. **Speed and heading.** A constant-velocity Kalman filter per track, in world coordinates.
5. **Real time.** ONNX export, a smaller input, detection on every second frame, and detection running alongside tracking.

## Experiments and results

| Pillar | Data (each test split run once) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A: tracking | VisDrone test-dev | Identity F1 (IDF1) 0.760 vehicles, 0.436 people |
| B: ranging | Mid-Air, 9 test flights (synthetic) | On the 78% of samples where both are valid: median error 2.4% (terrain from motion) against 14.7% (flat plane, true height); 90th percentiles 35% and 64%. Lower median on 8 of 9 flights |
| B: real footage | AU-AIR held-out flights | Repeatability 7.6% of range (no ground truth, so repeatability, not accuracy); detector AP50 only 0.21 (vehicles) and 0.02 (people) |
| C: speed | Laptop CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 5700U with Radeon Graphics) | 9.6 fps at IDF1 0.617; 33.4 fps sustained at IDF1 0.536 (validation) |

Figures: `results/midair/test/figures/` (error against depression and slope), `results/auair/figures/`, `results/edge/figures/pareto.png`.

**What I tested, and what I found.**
- **H1, off-the-shelf models degrade on aerial footage and adapting them recovers part of the loss: partly supported.** On validation, mean IDF1 went from 0.272 (pretrained, ByteTrack) to 0.316 with camera-motion compensation, and to 0.620 after fine-tuning and tuning. Tiled inference did not help tracking (0.539). I compared the baselines on validation only; test-dev ran once, for the final setting.
- **H2, error grows towards the horizon as propagation predicts: supported.** First-order and Monte Carlo predictions match the measured noise effect above 5° of depression; below 2° the error becomes non-linear (Monte Carlo 10 times first order).
- **H3, the uncertainty is calibrated, or can be made so with one scalar, and a flag catches the worst errors: partly supported.** Sensor noise alone is far too confident (standard deviation of the standardised error 11.4 for the flat plane, ideal 1), because the ground's shape dominates, and one scalar cannot fix that. Conformal calibration brings 90 % intervals to 84%; the flag's area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) is 0.68.
- **H4, the flat-ground assumption breaks on slopes: supported.** Flat-plane error grows from 6.4% to 23.7% with slope; terrain from motion stays at or below 3.7% up to 45°.
- **Robustness to navigation error (added after the test run, on development flights): the method needs accurate frame-to-frame poses.** Against 2.7% with exact poses on these flights, a shared error barely matters (a 5 m GPS offset leaves 2.7%; flat ground goes to 67%), but per-frame noise does: 2 cm of position noise gives 6.5%, 10 cm gives 18%, worse than flat ground with the true height. Ranging a detected car's box rather than a ground point adds a 3% short bias (5.6% end to end with exact poses). Lens distortion and rolling shutter are not modelled.
- **H5, real time on a CPU at a small accuracy cost: partly supported.** I reached 30 frames per second in throughput (33.4), but not in per-frame delay (47 ms median), and validation IDF1 fell from 0.617 to 0.536.

## Where it breaks

On real footage the detector transfers poorly (AP50 0.21 for vehicles), so many vehicles are never ranged. Near the horizon, where the error becomes non-linear; on slopes above 45°; on small people (16% tracked at 16 to 32 pixels tall); in the tail of terrain-from-motion errors (one in ten above 35% on the shared samples); and on real footage, where I had to infer the camera model and 11% of vehicle speeds are implausible. The full list is in `docs/limitations.md`.

## With real sensors

No test here runs the whole chain against known object distances; one flight past a car carrying a GPS logger, or a simulator with vehicles, would be the most valuable next test. Several of the largest error sources I measured would go away with better telemetry: a recorded camera tilt and lens calibration, a referenced altitude, synchronised time stamps, and a terrain model. A laser rangefinder or radar would measure range directly. The per-object uncertainty here is what would let one filter weight the camera against the active sensor, and fall back to the camera when the active sensor drops out. I have not tested target hardware or thermal footage.
